glossary.meaning: A **ticket** in this project's work list: one piece of work with a number, an owner and a status.
A small store **inside the web browser** where a page keeps text between visits. It lives on one device and one browser, and clearing the browser's data erases it.

The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines**, version 2.2, level AA: the accessibility level most public websites aim for. Normal-size text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background.
How much lighter the background is than the text, from 1 to 1 (no difference) to 21 to 1 (black on white). Low-contrast text is hard to read in sunlight and for people with weaker eyesight.

questions.title: Where should a shopping list be kept?
questions.plain: Today every list is kept only in the browser that created it, in its [localStorage](#g-localstorage). Nothing is sent anywhere, so nobody else can read the lists. But a list made on your phone is not on your laptop, and clearing the browser's data deletes every list without a warning.

head: Where the list lives
Survives clearing browser data
Same list on phone and laptop
Needs an account
rows: Browser, plus a file you export

questions.example: Sam writes the weekend list on the laptop on Friday. On Saturday in the shop, the phone shows last week's list, because the two browsers keep separate lists.

options.label: Keep lists on the server.
options.effect: Lists follow you to every device and survive clearing the browser. Everyone signs in once with an email link; about a week of work.

options.label: Keep lists in the browser only.
options.effect: Nothing changes, and no account is needed; the lost-list problem in the example remains.

options.label: Browser only, plus Export and Import buttons.
options.effect: No account; you move a list by hand as a file, and a copy you exported survives clearing the browser.

questions.title: Make the grey hint text darker?
questions.plain: The hint inside the empty input ("Add an item, e.g. 2 lemons") is light grey on white, a [contrast ratio](#g-contrast-ratio) of about 2.2 to 1. [WCAG 2.2 AA](#g-wcag-2-2-aa) asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for text of this size. Compare the two versions below.

figures.alt: The list screen with a very light grey hint in the empty input
figures.label: Before
figures.caption: Hint text in light grey, about 2.2 to 1.

figures.alt: The same screen with a darker grey hint that is easy to read
figures.label: After
figures.caption: Hint text in darker grey, 4.5 to 1.

options.label: Use the darker grey.
options.effect: Readable outdoors and meets WCAG 2.2 AA; the hint looks a little heavier.

options.label: Keep the light grey.
options.effect: Lighter look; hard to read in sunlight or with weaker eyesight.

progress.title: Quantities in grams and cups, built
progress.text: You asked for quantities in both metric units and cups and ounces. Each item now takes an amount and a unit, and a switch in the list's menu converts every amount at once. Tests cover the conversions for flour, sugar, butter and milk.
progress.action: open any list, press the menu, and try **Units: metric / cups and ounces** on a list with flour and milk.

questions.title: Which units should a new list start with?
questions.plain: A new list needs a starting unit system before anyone touches the switch.
questions.example: A visitor from Chicago opens the app for the first time and adds "sugar". With metric first, the amount box says grams; with the browser's region, it says cups.

options.label: Follow the browser's region.
options.effect: Visitors in the United States get cups and ounces; everyone else gets grams and millilitres. Usually right; wrong for a traveller.

options.label: Always metric.
options.effect: The same for everyone; visitors used to cups switch once.

options.label: Ask on the first visit.
options.effect: Always right, at the cost of one extra question before the first list.
